480.bp: Knowledge graphs—giant databases of facts organized as connections between things—are becoming enormous and need testing before deployment. Real-world testing with large, realistic graphs is expensive and slow, so researchers need artificial graphs that behave like real ones to stress-test systems and measure performance.
480.wh: When you build a fake knowledge graph by copying individual facts (triples), you lose the hidden shape of how those facts relate at higher levels. Real graphs have dense clusters and structures that matter, but most fake generators just stitched together random facts, creating artificially simple worlds that don't test systems properly.
480.ap: This work treats facts not as isolated points but as shapes. They look for geometric structures called simplices (imagine pyramids of connected facts) inside real graphs, then use the patterns of these higher-dimensional shapes to grow synthetic graphs that maintain realistic geometry. The generator preserves how facts naturally cluster and depend on each other.
480.ww: Simplices capture something triples alone cannot: how facts naturally group and reinforce each other. By learning these structural patterns first, the generator reproduces the dense, layered way real knowledge evolves, not just random collections of true statements.
480.po: The synthetic graphs they made passed structure tests 26% closer to real graphs than the best competing approach, and when used to test database engines, they gave query performance numbers only 6% off from real graphs—credible enough to predict how systems will actually perform.

481.bp: Finding tight communities in networks—groups of people who know each other, genes that work together—is central to understanding social media, biology, and the web. But real networks are enormous; checking every possible group is computationally impossible.
481.wh: A quasi-clique is a group where most connections exist but not all; it's more realistic than requiring perfect cliques. The edge-based version says a group is tight if its internal links exceed a density threshold. The math problem is NP-hard (no known fast solution), and unlike simpler problems, pruning tricks that work elsewhere don't apply here—you can't safely throw away partial solutions.
481.ap: The researchers split the dense subgraph-finding problem into smaller, hereditary pieces (each piece keeps the property when you remove nodes). This split lets them use aggressive pruning: if a partial solution can't possibly reach the target density even optimistically, discard it. They also add heuristics to explore the most promising branches first, guided by which sub-trees matter most.
481.ww: Hereditary subproblems let standard pruning work: many branches lead nowhere, and ruling them out early saves work exponentially. The heuristic guides search toward high-density regions where tight groups actually live, avoiding dead ends.
481.po: On 253 real networks, their algorithm EQC-Pro is up to 10,000 times faster than prior methods, making it practical to find communities in graphs with millions of nodes—fast enough to analyze real social and biological networks interactively.

482.bp: Events happen in sequences everywhere: people click items, patients visit clinics, earthquakes trigger aftershocks. Predicting the next event or spotting unusual patterns saves money (fraud, server failures) and lives (disease outbreaks). Current models either assume rigid math (Poisson: events at random rates) or hide their reasoning.
482.wh: Rigid mathematical models fail on real sequences where the past influences the future in complex ways—one event makes the next more or less likely, and different event types interact unpredictably. Neural models are flexible but treat interactions as invisible patterns inside matrices, so you can't debug or trust them. You don't learn what drives a prediction.
482.ap: This work splits the sequence model into two visible parts. The first layer learns how each event type evolves over time on its own, preserving its unique rhythm. The second layer explicitly models how different event types affect each other using a graph-like connection structure, making each interaction traceable. Irregular timing gaps between events are handled by separate time-encoding mechanisms for different scenarios.
482.ww: By making interactions explicit instead of buried in neural layers, the model becomes interpretable: you can see which event types reinforce each other and which suppress each other. This mirrors how real causality works. Separate time encodings let the model handle both regular and chaotic timing.
482.po: The model predicts future events more accurately than prior neural approaches and actually lets analysts understand why: which past events drove this prediction. This matters for critical domains like healthcare where doctors need to understand the system's reasoning.

483.bp: Web crawlers automatically discover and download pages from millions of websites to build search indices and monitor content. They have limited bandwidth (politeness rules, budget caps) and must choose which starting points to use to hit the most new pages, fastest.
483.wh: Today's crawlers rely on humans manually curating seed lists—picking entry points by guessing or habit. Humans pick either too many copies of the same redundant starting point or miss high-value ones entirely. No automated system learns from past crawls to predict which seeds will pay off.
483.ap: The system watches the crawler's own history—which seeds led to new discoveries versus dead ends—and learns two measures per seed: stability (do the links stay available across runs?) and productivity (how many new pages does this seed find?). It then greedily ranks seeds by combined value, maximizing total unique coverage within budget.
483.ww: By learning from real crawl history instead of guessing, the system adapts to each site's actual behavior. Ranking by marginal gain (how much new value does this seed add?) avoids redundant choices. The approach is greedy but effective: each step picks the seed that gives the most new coverage.
483.po: On 5,238 real websites, URLBank found more unique pages, used fewer seed requests, and discovered fresh content sooner than manual curation—all measurable gains deployed in Meltwater's production crawler. The system is auditable: operators can see why each seed was chosen.

484.bp: AI assistants now write code, but they make predictable mistakes: they get stuck on one idea, miss edge cases, and can be tricked by tiny input changes. Code with hidden biases, security holes, or logical flaws is dangerous in production. We need ways to catch these mistakes before code is deployed.
484.wh: Large language models think like a monolith: once they commit to an approach, they rarely backtrack or consider alternatives. They can't naturally spot their own blind spots, and standard testing misses flaws because LLMs are good at appearing confident even when wrong. Debate among multiple agents helps with efficiency, but doesn't fix the core reasoning blindness.
484.ap: This system creates three AI roles that argue: an Optimist pushes forward with the best case for each plan, a Pragmatist raises practical concerns, and an Adversarial Skeptic actively hunts for ways the plan fails. They debate and refine together. After convergence, a separate verification module intentionally breaks the plan with tricky inputs (changing numbers, flipping conditions) to stress-test it.
484.ww: Adversarial debate forces the model to articulate why a plan works, not just assert it. The skeptic voices doubts the monolithic model wouldn't generate alone. Counterfactual stress-testing (deliberately perturbing inputs) catches brittle code that works on examples but fails on variations—catching the hidden flaws.
484.po: The paper doesn't give full results in the abstract, but the method is designed to produce code that is functionally correct, less biased, and more resilient to tricky inputs by making the AI actively defend its reasoning against structured attacks.

485.bp: Cybercriminals send malicious network traffic (viruses, stolen data, attacks). Network switches can inspect packets at terabits per second to catch threats before they reach servers. But inspecting each packet requires balancing speed against accuracy: overly simplified checks miss attacks; complex checks slow the network.
485.wh: Machine learning detection models are complex (many decision rules), so they're simplified into decision trees for speed. A single pruned tree is fast but inaccurate (too many false negatives). Multiple trees are accurate but overload the hardware (too much wasted checking). No middle ground exists under the old design.
485.ap: This system splits a decision tree into critical and normal parts based on their importance to accuracy. Critical branches (the ones that matter most) run on the switch's fast hardware even if they're complex. Normal branches run elsewhere or are simplified. The system automatically minimizes coordination overhead so decisions are fast and complete.
485.ww: By treating branches unequally—giving resources to the ones that move the needle on accuracy—you avoid both extremes. Splitting lets the system adapt to available hardware: if the switch has room, keep critical rules; if it's full, migrate them elsewhere or simplify gracefully.
485.po: Proteus detects malicious traffic with high accuracy while using minimal switch resources, scaling to network speeds. It dynamically adjusts to changing hardware availability, keeping detection accurate even under resource pressure.

486.bp: Toxic content (hate speech, harassment) spreads on social media and harms users. Automated detection systems clean feeds in real time. But bad actors keep evolving their tricks—using typos, replacing letters with numbers, hiding slurs in slang—to dodge filters. Static detectors fail against evolving attacks.
486.wh: Detectors trained on today's tricks break when attackers invent new ones tomorrow. Retraining from scratch is slow and wasteful. Continual learning on new tricks sounds good but breaks down: each perturbation type has its own quirks; noise introduced by typos or tricks distorts meaning; and the detector becomes oversensitive to surface variations.
486.ap: This system uses an LLM to reconstruct the original meaning behind perturbations—expanding typos, explaining slang, recovering original intent—and enriches the noisy text with semantic clues about toxicity before checking. As new evasion tricks emerge, the detector learns from them incrementally without forgetting old ones, building robustness gradually.
486.ww: By recovering meaning before detection, the system separates the evasion noise from the actual toxic signal. Incremental learning lets it adapt to new tricks without retraining everything. Using an LLM to understand context makes the detector robust to surface-level tricks because it reads intent, not just letters.
486.po: ContiGuard detects toxic content that uses evolving perturbations, staying effective as attackers adapt. It maintains accuracy over time without full retraining, handling both old and new evasion tactics in production.

487.bp: Scientific papers, patents, and legal documents are increasingly digital and vast. Extracting meaning—who invented what, which laws apply—requires machines to read and organize this unstructured text with complex embedded charts and tables that current AI can't process automatically.
487.wh: Legal and scientific documents are messy: facts are scattered, tables contain crucial details that aren't in text, figures show relationships words don't capture. Treating documents as pure text loses structure. Knowledge graphs are rigid and incomplete. Large language models alone can't handle complex reasoning over structured knowledge.
487.ap: This workshop explores the intersection of three fields: semantic web technologies (structured knowledge), language models (understanding text), and reasoning systems (drawing conclusions). The goal is to investigate how structured knowledge representations can guide language models toward more reliable and understandable reasoning.
487.ww: Combining symbolic structure (knowledge graphs, logical rules) with statistical learning (LLMs) lets systems be both flexible and interpretable. Machines can extract meaning from messy documents by recognizing structure, then reason over that structure reliably. This hybrid approach avoids pure-text LLM errors.
487.po: Research at this workshop advances methods to extract and organize scientific and legal knowledge automatically, making vast document corpuses machine-readable and queryable—enabling faster discovery and more reliable compliance checking.

488.bp: AI models are shared online and used widely. If a model learns sensitive information (medical records, copyrighted text, private data), owners should be able to ask the model to forget it. Machine unlearning is the process of removing information from a trained model.
488.wh: Current tests check if the model still outputs the sensitive data—does it still complete 'John Smith is'? But testing output is insufficient: the model could have hidden the information internally while keeping knowledge of it dormant, ready to be recovered with the right prompt. Simply suppressing answers isn't true forgetting.
488.ap: This work uses sparse autoencoders (a decomposition technique) to peer into intermediate layers of the model and spot the hidden feature patterns representing each class. Then they use inference-time steering—nudging the internal activations—to test whether sensitive features can be recovered. If they can, suppression, not deletion, occurred.
488.ww: By examining internal representations rather than just outputs, you catch sneaky suppression: the model learned to hide sensitive answers but didn't truly forget the knowledge. Sparse autoencoders make internal features human-readable and testable. Steering lets you check if forgotten information is still accessible internally.
488.po: Testing 12 unlearning methods, they found most only suppress information at the decision boundary while keeping semantic features intact internally. Even retraining doesn't remove robust features from pretraining. This reveals critical gaps: unlearning methods need to delete representations, not just outputs.

489.bp: Recommendation systems chat with users to figure out what they like and suggest relevant items (movies, products, news). The system should learn from past conversations. But reusing old conversations blindly can backfire: a user who watched sad movies last month might want action movies today; yesterday's data misleads today's recommendation.
489.wh: Historical information helps detect patterns—frequent users, seasonal shifts—but also traps the system. Old dialogue sessions can cause cognitive negative transfer: forcing yesterday's preferences onto today's decision. The system needs to distinguish between helpful history (personal taste) and harmful history (outdated context).
489.ap: This system creates two simulated agents that debate whether old dialogue sessions help or hurt the current recommendation. A supporting agent argues for using each session; an opposing agent argues against it. After debate, only the vetted useful sessions are injected into the recommender's core parameters, personalizing it selectively.
489.ww: Debate creates a check on mindless history reuse. By forcing articulation of why past data helps (or doesn't), the system learns to filter. Parametric injection embeds only the vetted knowledge directly into the model, so the recommender naturally prefers recent, relevant signals over stale historical noise.
489.po: EyeCRS improves recommendation accuracy by selectively leveraging user history, using debate to screen out sessions that would mislead. It balances learning from past behavior with adapting to present preferences, a key tension in real recommendation systems.

490.bp: Recommendation systems need to rank items fast based on sequences of past user clicks. Attention-based models (the current standard) are accurate but slow: checking every past click against every candidate item costs quadratic time, making long user histories prohibitively expensive.
490.wh: Sequences of user clicks can be thousands of events long. Attention multiplies that length by the number of items to check, making both memory and compute quadratic—doubling sequence length quadruples work. No one can afford that at scale. Simpler models (recurrent networks) are faster but less accurate on real behavior.
490.ap: This system replaces attention with Hyena, a sub-quadratic operator (linear scaling with sequence length) that uses polynomial-based kernels to recognize long-range temporal patterns. A gating mechanism on top captures short-term behavioral bursts (quick click sequences). Together, they model both slow trends and fast changes with just linear computation.
490.ww: Polynomial kernels compress long-range dependency patterns into smooth, learnable functions instead of checking every past click individually. The gating layer handles the fine detail. This combination gives you the expressiveness of attention at linear cost by separating long-term and short-term reasoning.
490.po: HyenaRec outranks items as accurately as attention models but trains 6 times faster, with massive wins on long sequences where efficiency matters most. This makes recommendation practical for users with deep, complex click histories.

491.bp: Large language models can write and reason, but they forget conversations end-to-end, treat each query as isolated, and can't develop expertise or personality over time. Real assistants should remember what happened, learn from it, and improve their reasoning incrementally.
491.wh: LLMs have no persistent memory between conversations. They also lack structured organization—everything is just text in a massive context window. Coordination between multiple LLMs acting as specialized agents is ad-hoc. Deployed agents struggle to remember hundreds of interactions or update their knowledge dynamically.
491.ap: PromptX gives agents three layers. A prompt markup language lets you define personas and memory schemas (what to remember and how). Engrams—structured records of experiences—feed into a graph-based activation-diffusion network that links raw memories to conceptual summaries, enabling associative recall (thinking of a term bubbles up related memories). A protocol layer coordinates multiple agents using web standards (HATEOAS), letting new tools be discovered and invoked dynamically.
491.ww: Structured memory distinguishes raw experience from conceptual knowledge, so the system can generalize (this user is a developer) while staying grounded (this developer just mentioned Python). Graph propagation lets related memories reinforce each other: mentioning 'Python' activates memories about coding, which surfaces relevant advice. Dynamic tool discovery lets agents adapt without reprogramming.
491.po: PromptX deployed in 15+ enterprises over 5 months, accumulating 50K+ downloads and 3K+ GitHub stars. It demonstrated that agents with persistent, structured memory and dynamic coordination actually work in practice for diverse industries.

492.bp: Recommendation systems rank items by predicted relevance to a user. But the actual goal is simpler: deliver the top-K best items, not rank everything perfectly. Current models are trained to match this top-K ranking goal roughly, but their architecture doesn't actually optimize for it.
492.wh: Recommendation models are built around tasks like matrix factorization or graph neural networks—general-purpose designs not aligned with top-K ranking. They optimize auxiliary metrics (mean squared error, cross-entropy) as proxies for top-K performance. This misalignment means models learn patterns that don't serve the real goal.
492.ap: TopKGAT derives a recommendation architecture directly from the mathematical formulation of top-K metrics (Precision@K). Each forward pass through a layer approximately performs one gradient step toward maximizing Precision@K. The structure resembles graph attention networks but with layers explicitly shaped by the top-K objective.
492.ww: When your architecture's forward pass is literally gradient ascent on your goal metric, the model's learning is perfectly aligned with what you actually care about. You avoid the proxy-metric problem entirely: the model naturally learns patterns that boost top-K ranking, not patterns that look good on other metrics.
492.po: TopKGAT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on four benchmark datasets by ranking the most relevant items higher, with an architecture design that makes this outcome mathematically inevitable rather than hoped-for.

493.bp: Advertisers bid for clicks on ads; systems predict which users will click to allocate ads efficiently. But users' interests shift: someone researching apartments might click real estate ads today but ignore them tomorrow. Systems should adapt to these rapid swings, not just average past behavior.
493.wh: Current models learn from raw user history but overfit to historically dominant behaviors—what the user clicked last month matters too much. They also treat each ad candidate independently, ignoring that the full set of candidate ads on the page conveys context about what the user might want right now. This isolation discards crucial information.
493.ap: GenCI uses a generative model (trained to predict the next click) to produce candidate interest cohorts—groups representing the user's current, immediate interests, not their full history. These cohorts are semantic summaries, not just recent clicks. A ranking network then uses cross-attention to align these cohorts with both the candidate ad and the page context, refining the prediction.
493.ww: By generating current intent separately from historical behavior, the model can capture rapid interest shifts. Semantic cohorts are abstract enough to generalize (the user cares about 'home improvement' today) but concrete enough to guide ranking. Cross-attention lets the model adjust its view of user intent based on what's actually available to recommend.
493.po: GenCI improves click prediction by modeling dynamic user interest through semantic cohorts, avoiding both historical overfitting and myopic candidate-wise ranking. It aligns the model's internal representation with real-world ranking dynamics.

494.bp: Cities are deploying participatory platforms to let residents vote and propose ideas—but today's tools are basic (vote yes/no, fill forms). For real democracy at scale, residents need rich deliberation: proposal refinement, consensus-building, fair synthesis of competing views. This requires smarter tools, not just better voting.
494.wh: Large language models can draft text and summarize, but they're black boxes—no one knows how they weighted opposing views or why they recommended one idea over another. Using an autonomous LLM for civic decisions risks algorithmic bias and erodes trust. People need to understand and contest the system's reasoning.
494.ap: This work proposes a framework that explicitly bounds when and how LLMs are used in four civic stages: drafting (LLM helps format resident proposals), convergence (LLM identifies common ground), synthesis (LLM summarizes themes), and moderation (LLM flags norms violations). Each stage specifies transparency requirements, letting residents audit decisions and contests biased outputs.
494.ww: By limiting LLM autonomy to specific stages and requiring transparency at each stage, the system preserves human agency and accountability. Residents can understand why an idea was categorized as 'transportation' or flagged as off-topic. Contestation mechanisms let people challenge algorithmic decisions, making the system legible instead of opaque.
494.po: The paper provides a roadmap for integrating LLMs into civic platforms while maintaining democratic legitimacy. It identifies design constraints that prevent automation bias, enabling genuine deliberation at scale rather than replacing democracy with algorithmic efficiency.
